s15.slug: THURSDAY · 10:12 AM · DELGADO HALL → THE LAGOON PATH — ONE UMBRELLA

body.text: 5 to 4. i read the whole syllabus in bed. picking you up at 10. youre explaining it while we walk

body: It rained all night, and in the morning it rains harder: the big one, the one the radio has been promising since Sunday, coming in off the Channel sideways, so that the eucalyptus along the Grove lean over and roar and let go of limbs onto the walk. The creek that runs dry under the Grove path eleven months of the year came up over the footbridge sometime before dawn and took the path with it. From the Delgado steps Jack can see the brown water going through the trees, fast, carrying bark.

He has Theo’s umbrella, because Theo left it on his bed yesterday and hasn’t been back for it: black, enormous, a handle of real cane, and the name of a shop on a street in London stamped in gold on the strap.

Skye comes up the walk from the lot in a yellow fisherman’s slicker three sizes too big, the hood up and rain dripping off the end of her nose, carrying two coffees in a cardboard tray that is going soft in her hands. She gives him one. With the hand that’s free she takes the umbrella away from him, opens it over the two of them with a snap, and looks up into it.
“This is Ted’s,” she says. “He’s had this since he was fourteen. He used to fence people with it at wrap parties.”
“It’s ten minutes to Morro.”
“Not the way we’re going.” She hooks her arm through his under the umbrella and turns him, away from the Grove, toward the Lagoon. “I didn’t drive over here to drive. Walk. Explain.”

So they take the long way, out along the Lagoon, where the path runs on a low bank between the water and the bluff and they are the only two fools out on it. The Lagoon has come up over its reeds. The rain pocks it out to the far shore, and the wind off the ocean pushes little brown waves across it backwards, toward the dorms.

He starts where the case started, because that’s the only way he knows how to explain anything. A nonprofit called Citizens United made a movie in 2008, *Hillary: The Movie*, ninety minutes of people on camera saying she shouldn’t be president, and they wanted it on cable, on demand, during the primaries. And McCain-Feingold said no corporation could pay to put anything on TV or cable that named a candidate inside thirty days of a primary. “So it was a crime,” he says, “to show a movie.”
“A movie paid for by a corporation.”

“Everything’s paid for by a corporation. The *Times* is a corporation.” He has the coffee in one hand and her arm in the other, and he’s walking and talking at once, which is the point. “In ’04, Wisconsin Right to Life wanted to run an ad on the radio telling people to call their two senators about the judges. Just call them. And it was illegal, because it said the senators’ names inside the window. They had to go to the Supreme Court to be allowed to say two names on the radio. They won, in ’07. For that one ad.” A gust comes across the water and she leans the umbrella into it without breaking stride. “And the Church is a corporation. Your archbishop’s a corporation. Legally. The Roman Catholic Archbishop of Los Angeles, a corporation sole. One man in a miter, incorporated. The NAACP’s a corporation. Pop’s Local —” He hears where it’s going and goes anyway, because it’s true. “The UAW can spend now too. Same as anybody.”
Skye stops walking. Under the umbrella that means he stops too, or drowns.
“I’m a corporation, Jack,” she says. “I’ve been a corporation since I was twelve.”
“You’re a —”

“My mother incorporated me. Skylark Pictures, Inc.” She starts off again and he has to lunge to stay under. “She named me a bird with a tax ID. Every check I’ve ever earned goes to Skylark, and Skylark pays me an allowance, and Skylark has an accountant in Encino I’ve met twice. Skylark gave five hundred dollars to a city councilman once. I found out at Thanksgiving.” She drinks her coffee. “And Meridian writes checks to both parties every two years, so whoever wins takes the call. I’ve been to the dinners. They put the girl from the show at the middle table, by the flowers, so the donors can say they sat with Cassidy.”
The rain comes across the Lagoon in one long sheet and hits the umbrella all at once, loud as gravel.
“I know what money does in a room,” Skye says. “I’ve been the centerpiece.”

Water strings off the ribs of the umbrella all around them, and he looks down at the top of the yellow hood and doesn’t have anything for it. Her thumb goes to the plastic lid of her coffee and pushes the little tab back and forth. The thumb from the wheel. He doesn’t fill the quiet; he’s learned that much.
“So who’s right?” he says.

“Stevens is right.” She looks up. “He’s eighty-nine. He’s the grandfather at Thanksgiving who’s right about everything, and everybody passes the potatoes over his head. He read part of it out loud from the bench this morning. You don’t do that unless you want the room to hear you lose.”

And she does them. She does Kennedy and Stevens as an old married couple who have been fighting over the same thermostat for decades: Kennedy earnest and wounded, from Sacramento, one hand flat on his heart; Stevens small and bow-tied and ancient and perfectly sure.
“*John. It’s freezing in this house.*”
“*It’s sixty-eight, Anthony. It’s been sixty-eight since Ford.*”
“*The thermostat has a right to be heard.*”
“*Anthony. It can’t vote.*”

She lets go of his arm long enough to get the white phone out of the slicker, the opinion still up on it from bed, and holds it in under the umbrella, beaded with rain. “This part’s real,” she says. “I’m quoting.” And in Kennedy, eyes shut, hand on the heart, off the wet glass: “*If the First Amendment has any force, it prohibits Congress from fining or jailing citizens, or associations of citizens, for simply engaging in political speech.*”

She scrolls a long way down with her thumb. “Also real.” And Stevens, very slow, very old, from somewhere down around her collarbone: “*Corporations have no consciences, no beliefs, no feelings, no thoughts, no desires.*” The phone goes back in the slicker. Still Stevens: “*Neither does the thermostat, Anthony. Put on a sweater.*”
He laughs so hard he lets go of her arm and walks out from under the umbrella into the rain, and she reels him back in by the Carhartt.

At the Lagoon bridge the wind finds them. It comes straight up the outlet off the beach, and Theo’s umbrella goes inside out with a crack, every rib at once, and tears half off its spokes and flaps over their heads, black and useless and pouring water onto them harder than the sky is. Skye looks up into the wreck of it. There’s no closing it now. She brings it down wrong side out, and puts it over her shoulder, and carries it off the far side of the bridge like a trophy.

They walk the rest of it under nothing. The rain gets down his collar and into his shoes, and her hood fills and spills, and he can’t leave the thing alone, because what he said was true and so is the other thing.

“Leo the Thirteenth,” he says. “Eighteen ninety-one. He says a handful of very rich men had laid a yoke on the poor that was hardly better than slavery. He says a worker has a right to band together with other workers, because on his own he hasn’t got a chance.” He wipes his face with a wet sleeve, which doesn’t help. “So the Local gets to talk. And Meridian gets to talk. And Exxon gets to talk more than both of them before lunch. And my father, who’s been laid off since June, gets a vote and a lawn sign.” He stops. “I just argued myself into a corner.”
“You did. I watched the whole thing.”
“I think it’s right. The law was wrong; they were right to throw it out.” He looks at the Lagoon. “And I hate it.”
“You go back and forth on Thomas More,” she says, pointing the dead umbrella at him. “Go back and forth on Kennedy. I like you when you’re losing.”
Up the last of the bank toward Morro she walks backward in front of him, the umbrella on her shoulder and her face turned up into the rain, and holds one hand out at him, palm up. Go.

choices.text: “If the Local can spend, so can Meridian. That’s fair.”
choices.key: Under one umbrella you told Skye that if the Local can spend, so can Meridian.
response: “If the Local can spend, so can Meridian,” Jack says. “That’s fair.”
“*Fair*,” Skye says, “is a word for people who’ve never seen the invoice.”

He opens his mouth and finds nothing in it. She watches him find nothing, and turns around and walks forwards again up the bank, the umbrella bouncing on her shoulder. “One for the corporation,” she says. “The corporation is very happy.”

choices.text: “You’ve been in the room. I haven’t.”
choices.key: Under one umbrella you gave Skye the point: she’s been in the room, and you haven’t.
response: “You’ve been in the room,” Jack says. “I haven’t.”
She stops on the path in the rain. Water runs off the point of the yellow hood in a string.
“Say that at the next bridge,” she says. “I want to hear it with an echo.”

She comes back down the two steps between them and puts her cold wet hand inside the open Carhartt, on his chest, over his heart, and leaves it there in the downpour while a gull goes over them sideways in the wind. Then she takes his arm again, and they go on up the hill like that, very slowly, as if Morro will wait.

choices.text: “The problem isn’t the speech. It’s that nobody’s poor enough to be in the room.”
choices.key: Under one umbrella you told Skye the problem is that nobody poor is in the room.
response: “The problem isn’t the speech,” Jack says. “It’s that nobody’s poor enough to be in the room.”

She stops in the rain to look at him. The dead umbrella comes down off her shoulder and hangs from her hand, dripping on her sneakers, and she goes on looking at him, wet to the skin, until he has to look at the Lagoon.
“Nobody at those dinners was poor,” she says. “Not one person. Not even the waiters. The waiters were actors.” She takes his arm. “Put that in a paper. Don’t say I gave it to you.”

choices.text: “You’re a corporation that steals mints off pillows.”
choices.key: Under one umbrella you called Skye a corporation that steals mints off pillows.
response: “You’re a corporation,” Jack says, “that steals mints off pillows.”
“Allegedly.” And she’s Kennedy again, outraged, hand on the heart, on behalf of the mint. “*Mr. Costigan. The mint is an association of citizens.*”

Every twenty yards up the hill to Morro the mint gets another sentence of its defense — its long service, its freedom of association with the pillow, the chilling effect on mints everywhere — and he is laughing too hard by the doors to get them open, so she does it, with her hip, and the umbrella goes in first.

body: Rain sheets down the south wall of Morro 1100 from the floor to the ceiling, so the light that gets through the glass is white and moving, and the three hundred people in the bowl of the hall sit in it like people at the bottom of a swimming pool.

They come in at the top as Fenner reaches the lectern, the slicker shedding water on every step, Jack soaked from the hair down and leaving prints, the dead umbrella over her shoulder. Fenner is in the Tevas, with the coffee. He looks up the stairs at the two of them over the microphone.
“Pair forty-one,” Fenner says, in the Texas. “You’re wet.”
“Field data,” Skye says.
Somebody in the middle rows laughs. Fenner drinks his coffee and puts up a slide of a wave.

In the corner seat under the exit sign she wrings the hood of the slicker out onto the floor, which is not allowed, and stands the umbrella in the aisle wrong side out, where it drips. His notebook is wet through at the edges. Fenner talks about fetch: how far the wind has blown over open water before it gets to you, and how the longer the run of ocean and the longer the storm, the bigger what comes ashore. She takes his pencil, and in his margin, small, under the date, she writes *you argue better wet*. She gives the pencil back, folds her hands on the desk, and is a model student at Fenner.

Two rows down, a boy in a crew hoodie has his phone up over his shoulder, the lens turned back up the rows toward the corner under the exit sign, his thumb on the screen. Jack sees the lens, and the thumb. The slide changes to a storm off Japan. The phone comes down into the boy’s lap, and beside Jack, Skye writes *fetch* in his margin and draws a box around it.

The quarter is hers. The jukebox by the door takes it with the sound it makes for everybody, a swallow and a long mechanical think, and then Sam Cooke comes out of the speaker over the pie case, 1957, so easy he could be singing across a kitchen to somebody drying dishes. Skye walks back to the corner booth on the beat and slides in, and when Jack comes to the pass with a rack she mouths it at him through the window, every word, chin up, eyes shut on the long ones.

Outside, the storm has the wharf. It comes over the end of the pier in white sheets and runs back down the planks toward the street, and every time a big one lands the Anchor’s front windows shiver in their frames. Three harbor guys at the counter, waiting out the weather. A trucker with a newspaper. The door hasn’t opened since eight. Jack has been on since seven, and the dishes have been a trickle.

An hour ago Gloria set a slice of boysenberry in front of Skye, unasked, without slowing down, and Skye is eating it in small bites to make it last, with *Oceanography 1* propped open against the napkin dispenser at the chapter on fetch. Rudy is on the line in his hairnet, turning hash browns. The flat-top hisses. Rain runs down the window over the sink.

At nine Gloria goes into the office and comes back out with the Zenith off her desk held against her apron, the little one with the wood-grain sides and the channel dial, and sets it on the end of the counter by the register and runs the cord behind the pie case. “For storms and the World Series,” she says, to Jack, though he didn’t ask. She turns the dial through snow to the channel out of Los Angeles, and stands back with her arms folded, and a lake comes up on the screen, a boarding school on a lake, in fall, every window lit.
“My granddaughter got me started,” Gloria says. “I watch for the clothes.”
In the corner booth Skye puts her fork down.

On the screen Cassidy comes down a staircase in a white wool peacoat with toggles, carrying a thermos. It’s night at Sweetwater Academy, and it’s raining there too, and her roommate is in the boathouse with a packed bag, meaning to row across the lake in the dark and never come back. Cassidy finds her. Cassidy pours her cocoa out of the thermos. Cassidy says the lake will still be there in the morning, and so will she, and takes off the peacoat and puts it around the roommate’s shoulders, and the music comes up under it like a bath running.
“That coat’s real wool,” Gloria says. “They spent money on that girl.” She watches Cassidy tuck the collar up around the other girl’s ears. “That one’s a vanilla custard. Nice. Nothing in it.”
“I’ve been telling them that for three seasons,” Skye says from the booth.
Gloria turns her head as far as the corner booth, and then back to the screen. “Then tell ’em louder, hon. Somebody needs to put some lemon in her.”
“What am I?” Skye says.
“You I did already,” Gloria says, and goes down the counter with the coffee.

“My mother’s watching this right now in Studio City with a legal pad.” Skye has pulled her knees up onto the bench. “She’ll call me at seven tomorrow with notes. I had a cold in this one. Listen.” On the screen Cassidy says *you’re safe, sweetie, you’re safe*, softly, to the girl in the coat. “You can hear it on the *s*. Three days of honey and the *s* still went.”

She says *my mother* the way she always does, quick, already moving, a joke with the door shut behind it. He has learned not to follow her through that door with a question. He goes down the counter for the pot instead and fills her mug without being asked, and sets a second fork on the boysenberry plate so she has something to point at the screen with, and when he comes back from the pass she has stopped wincing at herself and started heckling.

Jack has never watched her on a screen with her in the room. He looks from the end of the counter to the corner booth and back: the girl in the white coat giving it away by a lake, all softness, every hair where somebody put it; and the girl in the booth with her knees up and his flannel on and purple on her bottom lip, mouthing her own lines a half-second ahead of herself and wincing at them. He likes the one in the booth so much it embarrasses him, at the pass, with a rack of cups in his hands.

At the flat-top Rudy has turned around with his spatula to scrape, and goes on scraping a grill that is already clean until the boathouse is over, with his eyes on the end of the counter. When Jack looks at him he goes back to his hash browns.

The harbor guys go out into it in a body before ten, and the Zenith is on the news with the sound down, and the Anchor is the trucker and the four of them and the storm. Skye comes up from the booth and sits on the last stool, by the pass, and puts an envelope on the steel shelf under the heat lamps and slides it through to him face up. One corner has gone soft from a week in her bag. On the front, in her block letters, it says TO DANNY COSTIGAN, and nothing else.
“I need the address,” she says. “I said that a week ago. I’ve been carrying him around.”

Jack takes the pen off the ticket wheel. Under her letters he writes DANIEL F. COSTIGAN, because the State of Ohio has never heard of a Danny, and after it the number, in his ordinary hand, small. He has known that number for two years. Under that he starts the second line: TRUMBULL CORRECTIONAL —

Rudy has come to the pass to set up the trucker’s plate. His eyes go down to the envelope on the steel as the second line goes onto it, and he turns back to the flat-top and picks up the spatula, and says it without turning around.
“Write the number big, *mijo*. They lose ’em if the number’s small.”
Gloria comes by for the trucker’s plate and reads the envelope upside down on her way past, like a ticket, and takes the plate.
Skye leans in over the steel to read the small number upside down.

journal.title: Gloria (the Anchor)
journal.text: Hired me for rating her pie a four. Rated me a lattice-top. I’m not going to ask. Told her I won’t be the next guy at the door. She says nobody holds a door that long without somebody else walking through it. Asked after the pecan. I said she’s seeing somebody, he’s nice. She said lattice-top. Boxed a pie for Nonna. From a woman who’s been on her feet thirty years. Peach is August. St. Nicholas Eve, at the end of my shift, low, at the pass: ‘Pecan came to see if you were here.’ Gave my Thursday to Hector — his girl’s due at Christmas. ‘Don’t argue with a baby.’ Says I look like the pie case at closing. Rated somebody new. Boysenberry. ‘That one’s not waiting for any door.’ The last night: two forks and the pecan, at the counter. ‘That one’s still standing in it, hon.’ Thursday I asked her for Saturday night. ‘Who’s she?’ ‘You met her.’ ‘Boysenberry.’ She gave it to Rudy’s nephew. Her granddaughter got her watching *Sweetwater*; Thursdays at nine, for the clothes. She rated Cassidy a vanilla custard. Skye agreed.

choices.text: *Write the number again, big. Tell her you know it by heart.*
choices.key: You addressed Skye’s letter to Danny from memory, number and all, big.
response: He goes back over the number, big, every digit twice the size of the one under it, and says it while he writes it, because she should have it: the letter and the six numbers. “I know it by heart,” he says. “Ma made us all learn it. It goes on everything she mails him. Birthday cards. The bulletin from St. Brigid’s.”
Skye leans over the shelf on her elbows to watch it go down, and says it back to him under her breath when he’s finished, the letter and the numbers, so she has it too.

response.text:

response: She takes it back from him and blows on the ink.

choices.text: “He’s going to think I hired you.”
choices.key: You told Skye Danny would think you hired her, and then you addressed it.
response: “He’s going to think I hired you,” Jack says.
“Tell him my rates.” She rests her chin on the steel. “Tell him I’m very expensive, and I did this one for nothing, because I liked his brother’s face.”
He goes back over the number, big, the way Rudy said, and finishes it.

response: She takes it through the window and tucks it into the front of the flannel, against her shirt, to keep it dry for later.

choices.text: *Tell her what Rudy means — everything’s read, and it’ll be the best day of his month.*
choices.key: You told Skye what Rudy meant: everything’s read, and it’ll be the best day of Danny’s month.
response: He tells her what Rudy means. That everything that goes in there gets opened and read by somebody at a desk before Danny ever touches it, so she should write it knowing that. That if the number’s wrong or small it sits in a bin. And that mail call is the best part of any day inside, and an envelope from a girl in California, printed big, from somebody he’s never met, is going to be the best day of his month. Maybe of his year. Danny will read it on his bunk till it’s soft.

Skye takes the envelope back. She turns it over, and with her other hand cupped around the pen like somebody keeping a match lit, she writes something on the flap, two lines, and he doesn’t see a word of it. She licks the flap again where it’s come unstuck and presses it down with her thumb and hands it back.
He goes over the number, big, his hand.

s18a.slug: THURSDAY · 11:00 PM · THE ANCHOR → THE FOOT OF THE WHARF → DELGADO HALL, THE CURB
body: The Zenith is the brightest thing left in the Anchor. Gloria has turned the sound up for the eleven o’clock news out of Los Angeles, and after the storm there is Conan O’Brien: NBC has made a deal to pay him something like thirty-two and a half million dollars to walk away, the newsman says, and money for his staff, and tomorrow night is his last show.
Jack, drying cups at the pass: “So somebody in Burbank meant something.”
“He meant it,” Skye says, from the last stool. “For thirty-two and a half million dollars.”

The weather comes on, the Central Coast in green and yellow and a red blot sitting on top of Marisol, and Gloria takes the towel off Jack’s shoulder. “The wharf’s going under,” she says. “Go before you do.”

The blue mailbox at the foot of the wharf stands in an inch of running water. Skye keeps the envelope inside the slicker till the last possible second, then pulls the slot open and feeds Danny in and lets the lid bang shut on him, and pats the box twice on its wet head, the way you’d see somebody off at a train.
“What did you put in it?” he says, in the Saab, with the top up and the windows gone white. “Danny’s.”
“That’s between me and Daniel F.” She puts it in gear. “He can tell you if he wants. Brothers tell each other everything. I’ve seen movies.”

At the curb at Delgado the wipers go and the heater runs, and she leans across the gearshift and kisses him, slow, her wet hair cold against his cheek and her mouth warm and tasting of boysenberry, the slicker creaking every time she moves. Up and down the street the rain comes down on the parked cars.
“Tomorrow,” she says, against his mouth. “His last show. My house.”

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom she isn’t allowed in and two boards under the porch the boys won’t let on the rack — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that. Picked my present for the church party: a Magic 8-Ball. Every answer’s a line reading, she says. Her car died in Buellton; I pushed. She’s seen Our Lady of Guadalupe on every taco truck in the Valley and thought she was a brand. Friday night she took my ‘right now’ apart, point by point, with visual aids, and made a very good case. It’s still right now. I said no again, and she stopped right there and nowhere else. Came to the Anchor in my shirt; Gloria rated her boysenberry. She’s going to ask every day, she says. It’s in her calendar. Slept at her house. Just slept. She says that doesn’t happen. Taught me to surf at Ellery on Gaudete Sunday. I’m terrible. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting. Played Hale in her car from my description. Made me answer the question I couldn’t at the Starlite. Thursday at one in the morning, no moon at all, she drove the bluff with the lights off. Not before Christmas, she said — Christmas and New Year’s and long distance are too much for something new. When I get back we’re dating. Officially. A whole thing. She counted. GM is killing Saab. I’m on the hook. Christmas week: Theo’s known her since they were eleven — his father’s company makes her show. She calls him Ted; nobody else does. She saw us walk into the Hallorans’ together and hid behind a ficus. “Peace mission” was for him. He ran into her at a party in the hills on the twenty-second, and she says he knows. She had me do the weather barefoot in the snow. Seventeen days; she’s not counting. Christmas morning my family found her — Gina gave me her show on DVD. They know her as the nice one. She wants it on her headstone. The day after Christmas my whole family watched season two of her show. She was eighteen, in a blazer, on a dock. She’s good — Dad said so, and she says nobody says good. Nonna prays for Cassidy now. She bought Chesterton used on Ventura without knowing it was my book, and wants to know who picked midnight. The Monday after Christmas she called, and we talked till my phone died. New Year’s Eve she watched my ball drop on the East Coast feed at nine her time and texted, so she’d be at midnight with me. Then she had her own, at three in the morning mine, from a locked den in the hills. I told her I called Ted *Ted*. She says he’s right: that one’s hers. She has my flight home written on her hand. She read Matthew 2 because I said Sunday was Epiphany; Herod is a jealous showrunner. OFFICIALLY, in eyeliner, on a sign at the rope at Santa Barbara, in sunglasses at night. A girl from my flight filmed it, and by morning it was on a gossip blog. Skye put the still on her own Facebook herself. Her people wanted lunch: her mother, Debbie, who manages her, and her publicist, Corinne. The rules: no pictures, ‘a friend from school,’ February. Take the airport down. She took it down. There was a folder with my last name on it, and she pushed it back without opening it. At a gas station in Buellton she took the first picture of the two of us herself, at arm’s length, and put it up instead. Then she changed her status herself and made me say yes to it on her phone — the first thing anybody ever watched her do that nobody wrote. Monday she came to the Fishbowl and argued with me about a rose. My pie got her out of remedial math. Tuesday she taught me stick in an empty lot — a voice for every stall. I do a bad Frank. We argued Conan. She posted a picture of me stalling. The radio, at 2:31: Haiti. At midnight she took the picture down — not for Corinne. Wednesday in the Brick she explained the plates under Haiti from her Oceanography book, read me Milton off the front of *Frankenstein*, and fell asleep on my shoulder. At the Haiti table she borrowed Becca’s apron and was Cassidy for twenty dollars a name, and asked me where God was at 4:53. Met Laney. Met everybody. Corinne wanted a statement; she told her the girl at the table was right about the pictures, and hung up. That night she asked me to say one for them, from her. ‘Saturday.’ Thursday Margot interviewed her at the Anchor; she says I’m the same in every room. Saturday at dawn she taught me again, inside the Point. Still very bad at it. She posted it and kept it up. She came to Sully’s and learned the Who Dat. Laney took a shot at her; she had it handled, she says, and I didn’t let her finish, and she says she’ll reward that sort of behavior. In the Saab I told her some about Lena — that we were close in the fall. She said she can tell there’s a rest. She drove me to confession, and went back to Sully’s without me. Saturday night she read me Sunday’s Gospel off her phone. Three nights in LA: a fitting for the wedding episode — she’s not the bride, she checked. Tuesday she made me explain Massachusetts while I walked. The tornado took Sol’s swing. Wednesday she drove home with the top down in the rain and put the two of us up on Facebook, soaked. Thursday we argued the Supreme Court under one umbrella until it turned inside out. She’s been a corporation since she was twelve — Skylark Pictures; her mother named it. She wrote my brother, in capitals; Rudy says write the number big.
